content:
Facts: The heirs of a deceased person challenged, on grounds of natural incapacity, the transfer of shares carried out by the deceased during his lifetime in favour of his brother and sought reduction for infringement of their legitimate shares. They also sought annulment of a notarial deed of division and, in the alternative, restitution for unjust enrichment.
Legal framework
Articles 428, 775, 782, 553–564, 2041–2042 ICC on natural incapacity, limitation periods, form of donations, reduction and unjust enrichment; Articles 183 and 190 CPC; Supreme Court case law on limitation periods for constitutive actions, burden of proof in actions for reduction, and distinction between nullity, annulment and reduction.
Interpretative issue
Whether actions for annulment based on natural incapacity were time-barred, whether the plaintiffs had standing to bring an action for reduction without acceptance with benefit of inventory, and whether a gratuitous transfer of registered securities could qualify as a valid (direct or indirect) donation capable of being reduced.
Principle applied
The action for annulment based on natural incapacity under Article 428 ICC is subject to a five-year limitation period running from the date of the act, irrespective of when the incapacity is discovered, and can be interrupted only by judicial action. An action for reduction is inadmissible if the legitimate heir has not accepted the inheritance with benefit of inventory where the donation was made to a third party, and in any event requires strict allegation and proof of the composition and value of the estate and of the extent of the alleged infringement. A direct donation of registered securities lacking the form of a public deed is null ab origine and cannot be the object of reduction; nor can the absence of consideration alone establish animus donandi. The subsidiary action for unjust enrichment is inadmissible where other specific remedies were available but allowed to become time-barred.
